job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the accounts office at Dunmore Builders' Supply in Sheffield, a family-owned timber and tool merchant. I started in October after my accounting degree. I process supplier invoices, match them to delivery notes and prepare the month-end statements for the credit customers. I share a rented flat with my cousin Samira, and we both go to my parents' home on Fridays for dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the order of it, and I like that the people at Dunmore have known each other for decades, like a big family. The difficult part is the first week of each month, when every builder wants their statement yesterday and phones to complain. My father runs a grocery shop, he's put some money aside for me, and he says a girl should have a trade in her hands. I have no debt, so I feel fortunate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, as my grandmother did about every new fashion, that it will pass. I'd tell my cousin and the people at Dunmore that good work comes from careful people. I wouldn't post about it, I keep my opinions for the family table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean nothing much changes, which is what I'd prefer. Dunmore has run on handwritten notes and phone calls for forty years, and Mr Hargreaves, the owner, doesn't like new things either. There are plenty of jobs for accountants in Sheffield, and I have over six months saved, so I'd feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish my AAT exams and keep building trust with the customers by phone. I'd save about a third of my pay and give a share to my mother for the family. And I'd go on seeing my parents every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. If the world stays the same, I know my place in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. What's your thinking behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I prefer to know how a number is made. When I check an invoice, I'm not only checking arithmetic, I'm checking that the supplier is honest. I wouldn't hand that to a tool that can't be held to account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the people around you would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop, in a way. My father's grocery is getting squeezed by the supermarkets, and he's tired. If it closed, I'd be the one helping the family, and I'd want to be sure of my own job. That's a worry I carry even in a calm world.

say: I'd say it will **pass**, like every new fashion my grandmother saw.
I'd tell colleagues good work comes from **careful people**.
think: Nothing much changes, which I **prefer**, and Dunmore runs on notes and phone calls.
There are plenty of **accounting jobs** in Sheffield, and I have savings.
do: Finish my **AAT exams** and keep building trust with customers by phone.
Save about a **third** of my pay and give a share to my mother.
feel: I feel **settled**, knowing my place in a world that stays the same.
S0.quote: When I check an invoice, I'm not only checking arithmetic, I'm checking that the supplier is honest.
fieldNote: Daria is **secure**, but the family grocery is a quiet worry.
She sees accounting as a **trust** job, not only a numbers job.
Her wish for **continuity** is strong and shapes every answer.

steps.text: Finish the AAT exams this year
Save a third of my pay each month
Give some pay to my mother for the household

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should not rush, and that anyone who loses work should be helped by their family and their community first. I'd tell colleagues that Dunmore should only change when it's proven. I wouldn't raise my voice, but I'd be clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my invoice matching is exactly what the card lists, checking and answering customers. A program could read delivery notes and match them in seconds. Dunmore doesn't have to fire me tomorrow, but it won't hire the next girl, and I worry about that. I also know I don't use these tools, which makes me slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hargreaves to move me to customer accounts, where people phone and I can calm them down. I'd learn the new invoice system when the firm adopts it, but only then, I won't chase new things. I'd also save more, £600 a month, and stay close to my family, because they'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little afraid and a little proud. Proud that I can say what I do is real work, afraid that it doesn't count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks at Dunmore would a program do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matching and checking would go first. The calls with customers who are arguing over a bill would stay a while longer, and so would the old customers who know my voice. I'd want to be the one they ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Mr Hargreaves react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hargreaves would be slow, which I like. He'd wait until another merchant did it, then follow. He'd probably say nobody loses their job, and then, when the old bookkeeper retires, there's no replacement. That's how it happens, quietly.

say: I'd say we should not **rush**, and family and community should help first.
I'd tell colleagues Dunmore should only change when it's **proven**.
think: My **invoice matching** is exactly what the card lists, and a program could do it in seconds.
Dunmore might not hire the **next girl**, and I don't use these tools.
do: Ask Mr Hargreaves to move me to **customer accounts**, where people phone.
Learn the new **invoice system** when the firm adopts it, not before.
Save **£600** a month and stay close to my family.
feel: I feel a little **afraid** and a little proud that my work is real.
S1.quote: Dunmore doesn't have to fire me tomorrow, but it won't hire the next girl, and I worry about that.
fieldNote: Daria expects **attrition**, not firing, and has a precise view of how it happens.
Her tool resistance is a **self-aware** weakness.
Family and **community** are her safety net, not government.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hargreaves to move me to customer accounts
Stay close to my family and ask my father for advice
Learn the new invoice system only when Dunmore adopts it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong that a few firms can decide this for the rest of us. I'd say we need communities, families and sensible laws, not handouts. I'd say it at the mosque, at work and at home, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes in 2028, and so do most office jobs. Everything I do is thinking work, checking and matching, which is the first part. The robots come in 2031, after, but Dunmore's yard, the forklifts and the timber lifting, are hands-on, so the firm itself lasts longer than my desk. That doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every pound I could, perhaps £900 a month, and I'd stop spending on clothes and eating out. I'd talk to my father about moving home to cut costs. I'd also ask Mr Hargreaves if I could help in the yard or the shop, work with my hands, since that comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid. I'd pray more, and I'd sleep badly. I'd also be angry, because I did everything right and the ground moved anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do, practically, in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It says we look after each other. My family would take me in, and I'd help my father with the shop. I'd never ask the state first, though I'd accept it if it came. We'd do what our community has always done, share what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your faith or your family say about a time like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the people who'd know, like the older accountants at the mosque and in the community. They've been through hard times. They'd tell me to be humble, keep working and keep faith.

say: I'd say it's wrong that a few firms decide this for everyone, and families need **sensible laws**.
I'd say it at **home** and in my community, plainly.
think: Privately, my job goes in **2028**, along with most office jobs.
Dunmore's **yard** lasts longer than my desk, but that doesn't save me.
do: Save **£900** a month and stop spending on clothes and eating out.
Talk to my father about **moving home** to cut costs.
Ask Mr Hargreaves about **yard or shop work**, which lasts longer.
feel: I feel **afraid** and angry, since I did everything right and the ground moved.
S2.quote: I did everything right and the ground moved anyway.
fieldNote: Daria turns first to **family and faith**, with state help a distant fallback.
She sees **hands-on** work at Dunmore as longer-lasting and plans to move toward it.
Her anger is **moral**: she followed the rules.

steps.text: Save £900 a month while the job lasts
Stop buying clothes and eating out
Move back to my parents' house to cut rent
Ask Mr Hargreaves about work in the yard or shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to prepare, with apprenticeships and family support. I'd argue we should reward work and not dependence, and that firms should keep training young people. I'd say it respectfully but firmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a few years of useful work, enough to build a base. By 2031 I'll be twenty-seven, maybe married, and I'd want something steady. I'd also expect the desk side of accounting to be thin by then, so I'd look for something in the community. I don't expect it to be easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my AAT and then the ACCA, because a qualified accountant who can give advice and sign things still matters, I hope. I'd move toward bookkeeping and advice for small family businesses, the shops and the tradesmen. I'd start learning the tools slowly, with Samira's help. I'd also save £700 a month and give some to my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but there's room to breathe. Five years means I can still plan a family around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is more time. What kind of work might you seek out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say get a skill that people need near you. He'd say a small business needs a bookkeeper who they trust, so be that person. He'd also say don't borrow, keep your savings, and don't marry in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference with two years is I can finish what I started. In two I'd just be surviving. With five years I can build something, and I think that's better for the soul.

say: I'd say we should prepare through **apprenticeships** and family support.
I'd argue we should reward **work**, not dependence.
think: I'd have a few years of **useful work**, enough to build a base.
The **desk side** of accounting will be thin by 2031.
do: Finish my **AAT** and then the ACCA qualification.
Move toward **bookkeeping and advice** for small family businesses.
Learn the tools **slowly**, with my cousin Samira's help.
feel: I feel **nervous**, but with room to breathe and plan a family.
S3.quote: With five years I can build something, and I think that's better for the soul.
fieldNote: Daria's plan is **community bookkeeping**, rooted in trust.
She accepts tools **slowly**, with a relative's help.
Her father's **advice** anchors her: skill, savings, no debt.

steps.text: Finish AAT, then start the ACCA qualification
Learn the invoice tools slowly with my cousin Samira
Offer bookkeeping to small family shops at weekends
Save £700 a month and give some to my mother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and families should use it to teach children trades and values. I'd say governments shouldn't hand out money without asking for something back. I'd say it with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's manageable. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, with a husband and perhaps two children. I'd still work, but maybe part time, from home. The big change would arrive, but I'd have a family around me to share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and build my accounting career, then raise a family. I'd save for a house with my husband, and keep our parents in mind. I'd also learn enough about AI to be sure it's honest, because someone has to check it. And I'd keep helping my father's shop with its books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, honestly. A decade is long enough to marry, have children and learn new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes in your life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that trust is the real asset. A tool can do arithmetic, but it can't be your neighbour. Be someone who can be relied on, and learn whatever you have to, without being afraid of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want younger relatives to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My life plans wouldn't change much. I'd still want a husband, children, a home. The job would just be one part of it, which is how I like it.

say: I'd say a decade is a gift, and families should teach children **trades and values**.
I'd say governments shouldn't give money without asking for something **back**.
think: I think it's **manageable**, and by 2036 I'd be thirty-two with a family.
The big change would arrive, but I'd have **family** to share it.
do: Build my **accounting** career, then raise a family.
Save for a **house** with my husband and keep our parents in mind.
Learn enough about **AI** to check that it's honest.
feel: I feel **peaceful**, because a decade is long enough to marry and learn.
S4.quote: A tool can do arithmetic, but it can't be your neighbour.
fieldNote: Daria folds the scenario into **family plans**, not career pivots.
She is willing to learn AI as a **checker**, a notable shift from never.
Her values are **trust and reliability**, in each answer.

steps.text: Build my accounting career at Dunmore
Plan a marriage and children in the next six years
Save for a house with my future husband
Learn enough about AI to check its work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it gives no time for families to adjust. I'd like the government to protect people who can't work, but mostly I'd want to rely on my family and community, with training and apprenticeships to help. And I'd like firms to treat their staff like family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are being told to adapt, and some of us don't want to. I'm not against change, but I would like it to be done with respect for people who built something already.

headlineQuote: People like me are being told to adapt, and some of us don't want to.
portrait: Daria, 22, is an **accounts assistant** at a family-owned builders' merchant in Sheffield, and never uses AI.
She is traditional and religious, and trusts **family and community** before the state.
Her invoice matching is the work she expects to fade, so she leans toward **customer accounts** and community bookkeeping.
Mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and she plans her life around family.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it gives families no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and training, with firms treating staff like family.
Government **protection** for those who can't work, but family first.
